title: The human microglial HMC3 cell line: where do we stand? A systematic literature review

subsections.subsection_title: Microglial Identity and Core Biological Features
subsections.content:
Microglia are the resident macrophages of the central nervous system and constitute a distinct myeloid population defined by yolk-sac origin, long-term self-renewal, and strong dependence on local CNS cues rather than continual replacement by circulating monocytes ref [3]. Their identity is now understood as both lineage- and environment-instructed: while they share core myeloid programs with other tissue macrophages, they also express a characteristic molecular repertoire that distinguishes them from peripheral monocytes and other neural cells, including markers such as P2RY12, TMEM119, GPR34, CX3CR1, HEXB, and SALL1 ref [1], ref [2], ref [3].

A major advance in defining microglial identity was the demonstration that transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) signaling is essential for acquisition and maintenance of a mature homeostatic signature. In mice, TGF-β-dependent programs support expression of canonical microglial genes and functional quiescence, whereas commonly used microglial cell lines fail to recapitulate this adult signature ref [1]. Human studies further showed that microglial identity is rapidly eroded outside the brain milieu, with extensive loss of microglia-enriched transcripts and enhancer activity after transition to in vitro culture, emphasizing that microglia are specified by an environment-dependent transcriptional network rather than by ontogeny alone ref [2].

Beyond identity markers, core biological features of microglia include high motility, phagocytosis, trophic support, and immune sensing. These functions are mediated by specialized receptor systems, including TREM2/DAP12, which is highly expressed in microglia and has been implicated in lipid sensing, phagocytic activation, and survival-related signaling ref [4]. Early localization studies already highlighted strong TREM2/DAP12 expression in microglia within human and mouse brain tissue ref [4], and later molecular profiling placed TREM2 among the central components of the conserved microglial program ref [1], ref [2]. Together, these findings frame microglia as a uniquely CNS-adapted immune population whose phenotype is stable only within the appropriate tissue context.

subsections.subsection_title: Homeostatic Roles in Neural Circuit Development and Maintenance
subsections.content:
Beyond their canonical immune functions, microglia are integral to the construction and stabilization of neural circuits during development. In vivo imaging showed that so-called resting microglia continuously survey synaptic elements and make brief, activity-dependent contacts with both pre- and postsynaptic structures, indicating that homeostatic surveillance is tightly coupled to local neuronal function ref [5]. This synaptic engagement is further shaped by experience: in juvenile visual cortex, altered sensory input changes microglial process motility, synaptic apposition, and phagocytic behavior, supporting a role for microglia in experience-dependent circuit remodeling rather than passive monitoring alone ref [6].

A central homeostatic function of microglia is developmental synapse elimination. Direct evidence that microglia engulf synaptic material and are required for normal pruning came from studies showing increased spine density, excess PSD95-positive puncta, and delayed maturation of hippocampal circuitry when microglial CX3CR1 signaling is disrupted ref [7]. Complement-dependent mechanisms provide an additional molecular framework for this process, with classical complement components tagging weak or inappropriate synapses for removal during retinogeniculate refinement (Stevens et al., 2007). Together, these findings established microglia as active sculptors of connectivity whose actions are necessary for normal brain development ref [7].

Microglial homeostatic roles also extend beyond synapse removal to support of progenitor niches and glial maturation. In the early postnatal subventricular zone, activated microglia promote both neurogenesis and oligodendrogenesis through cytokine-dependent signaling, indicating that microglia help coordinate the production of neuronal and oligodendroglial populations needed for circuit assembly and maintenance ref [5]. Consistent with this broader trophic role, microglia-derived cues can direct neural precursor migration and differentiation in vitro (Aarum et al., 2003), emphasizing that microglia contribute to circuit homeostasis through balanced pruning, surveillance, and support of ongoing cellular renewal ref [5].

subsections.subsection_title: Experimental Models and Methods for Studying Microglia
subsections.content:
Microglia have been studied across a spectrum of experimental systems, each imposing distinct biological constraints. Primary cultures remain the closest reductionist model to native cells, but isolation strategy itself can alter phenotype. In rodent mixed-glial preparations, mild trypsinization yields higher purity and a more quiescent, ramified baseline state than shaking, which can partially pre-activate cells and modify cytokine release and phagocytic behavior ref [9]. In human material, early primary studies established that brain-derived macrophage/microglial cultures can be isolated from fetal CNS tissue and distinguished from circulating monocytes by marker expression and functional properties, underscoring the value—but also the scarcity and developmental specificity—of human primary preparations ref [11].

Because access to human primary microglia is limited, immortalized lines have been developed to improve experimental throughput and reproducibility. An early example, the HMO6 line, retained multiple microglial/macrophage markers, phagocytic capacity, ATP-responsive calcium signaling, and inducible cytokine/chemokine programs broadly comparable to primary human microglia, illustrating the utility of transformed human models for mechanistic studies ref [10]. Such lines enabled systematic interrogation of inflammatory stimuli, including LPS and amyloid-β, but also highlighted that immortalization and culture adaptation can shift specific response axes relative to primary cells ref [10]. These considerations are directly relevant to HMC3, which is widely used precisely because it offers a practical human microglial platform, yet must be interpreted as a context-dependent surrogate rather than a full equivalent of adult homeostatic microglia.

Methodologically, microglial studies now combine immunophenotyping, phagocytosis assays, calcium imaging, ELISA, and transcript analyses to benchmark model fidelity ref [9], ref [10], ref [11]. Equally important is quality control: cell-line authentication and routine mycoplasma testing are minimum requirements, since misidentification and occult contamination can profoundly distort inflammatory readouts and reproducibility ref [6]. STR profiling and PCR-based mycoplasma screening are therefore best viewed not as optional technical add-ons, but as essential components of any rigorous workflow using immortalized microglial models, including HMC3 ref [6].

From a translational perspective, HMC3-like human microglial systems have been used to evaluate druggable signaling nodes that couple inflammatory activation to survival and motility. In the neurotensin axis, human microglia express NTR3/sortilin, and neurotensin promotes migration through PI3K/Akt and ERK signaling, highlighting receptor-proximal pathways that are pharmacologically tractable in human cells ref [8]. Extending this framework, neurotensin was later shown to drive proinflammatory cytokine/chemokine release and microglial proliferation through sortilin-dependent mTOR activation, effects suppressed by rapamycin-class inhibitors and by the flavonoid methoxyluteolin, suggesting a candidate intervention route for neurodevelopmental disorders with microglial involvement ref [13].

A second translational theme is the repurposing of survival-pathway inhibitors to eliminate long-lived infected myeloid reservoirs. In HIV-1 models that included human microglial or macrophage-like cells, infection or Tat expression activated PI3K/Akt signaling, lowered PTEN, and conferred stress resistance; pharmacologic inhibition of this pathway selectively sensitized infected cells to death while reducing viral output ref [9], ref [10]. Notably, clinically oriented alkylphospholipids such as miltefosine, perifosine, and edelfosine suppressed Akt/GSK3β signaling and promoted death of HIV-expressing macrophage/microglial models, supporting host-directed strategies against persistent CNS-associated reservoirs ref [10].

These studies also illustrate the utility of immortalized human microglial lines for phenotypic drug discovery. A Tat-dependent survival assay in CHME5 cells enabled the identification of additional PI3K/Akt-modulating compounds, including lancemaside A1, compound K, and arctigenin, which interfered with distinct steps of the pathway ranging from PI3K activity to Akt membrane recruitment and phosphorylation ref [11]. Collectively, such work positions human microglial cell lines as useful preclinical platforms for target validation, mechanism-of-action studies, and early prioritization of host-directed anti-inflammatory or antiviral candidates, while also underscoring the need for subsequent confirmation in primary human microglia and more physiologic CNS models ref [13], ref [9].

subsections.subsection_title: Microglia in Neuroinflammation, Infection, and Disease
subsections.content:
Microglia are central effectors of neuroinflammation in infection and neurodegeneration, but HMC3-based studies also show that their inflammatory outputs are strongly model- and stimulus-dependent. A notable example is constitutive NOX4 expression in HMC3, which drives intracellular reactive oxygen species production and sustains basal IL-6 expression, suggesting a chronic oxidative-inflammatory bias even in the absence of classical activation ref [20]. In the HIV context, Tat further amplifies this redox axis by suppressing miR-17 and increasing NOX2/NOX4 expression and ROS generation, linking viral proteins to microglial oxidative stress and cytokine dysregulation ref [21].

HMC3 and related human microglial models have also been used to dissect pathogen-sensing pathways. Hepatitis C virus NS3 induces IL-8, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β through a TLR2/TLR6-MyD88-NF-κB cascade, while prior exposure to selected TLR ligands can induce a tolerized state associated with reduced pro-inflammatory output and increased IL-10, highlighting the context dependence of innate signaling ref [11]. Viral infection studies likewise reveal bidirectional microRNA control: miR-155 overexpression in human microglial cells suppresses Japanese encephalitis virus replication while attenuating IRF8, STAT1, and NF-κB-linked innate responses ref [13]. In HIV reservoir models, microglia support proviral persistence and can be experimentally manipulated; engineered microglial lines have been used to model inducible proviral activity ref [15], and TLR3 stimulation selectively reverses HIV latency in microglia, underscoring a distinctive intersection between antiviral sensing and reservoir biology ref [20].

Beyond infection, microglial inflammatory programs are also relevant to chronic neurodegenerative disease and toxic injury. In human microglia, amyloid-β42 and lipopolysaccharide trigger qualitatively different resolution programs, with amyloid exposure appearing less effective at engaging pro-resolving pathways than bacterial stimulation ref [12]. Environmental toxicant paradigms add a further disease-relevant layer: chronic low-dose rotenone alters human microglial viability and inflammatory phenotype, supporting the use of these systems for Parkinson-related neuroinflammatory modeling ref [19]. Collectively, these studies position HMC3-like models as useful, though imperfect, platforms for probing how infection, oxidative stress, amyloid pathology, and toxic injury converge on microglial dysfunction in CNS disease ref [20], ref [15].

subsections.subsection_title: Cell-Cell Interaction and Microenvironmental Shaping of Phenotype
subsections.content:
HMC3 phenotype is highly context dependent and is reshaped by direct contact with other neural cell types. In an allogeneic co-culture model with human neural stem/progenitor cells (NPCs), HMC3/CHME3 cells displayed increased survival and proliferation, enhanced latex-bead phagocytosis, and a shifted surface phenotype characterized by higher HLA-II and CD206 expression, indicating that neighboring progenitors can simultaneously reinforce antigen-presentation and reparative features rather than driving a simple binary polarization state ref [26].

The same co-culture study also showed reciprocal microenvironmental instruction: NPCs increased microglial CD200R expression, while microglia increased NPC CD200, alongside elevated TGF-β release, consistent with an immunoregulatory contact-dependent axis that can dampen excessive activation and favor a repair-supportive niche ref [26]. More broadly, chemokines are central organizers of such microenvironmental crosstalk, governing not only chemotaxis but also adhesion, chemokinesis, haptotaxis, and retention, with signaling further shaped by glycosaminoglycan binding, receptor promiscuity, and atypical chemokine receptors ref [7]. In the CNS, chemokines mediate communication among neurons, astrocytes, and microglia and can switch from beneficial to detrimental functions depending on timing and inflammatory load ref [8].

A further layer of niche conditioning is provided by protease activity. Metalloproteinases in myeloid cells regulate extracellular-matrix turnover, receptor ectodomain shedding, chemokine processing, and migratory behavior, thereby controlling how cells perceive and remodel their surroundings ref [9]. For HMC3, this framework is particularly relevant because matrix-remodeling enzymes and chemokine networks likely determine how closely the cell line approximates surveillance, antigen-presenting, or wound-response states under different co-culture or conditioned-medium paradigms. Overall, available evidence argues that HMC3 should not be interpreted as having a fixed basal phenotype, but rather as a plastic in vitro sensor-effector population whose identity is strongly molded by local cellular and extracellular context ref [1,7–9].

subsections.subsection_title: Microglial Identity and Basal Molecular Signature of HMC3 Cells
subsections.content:
Assessment of HMC3 microglial identity must be framed against contemporary definitions of bona fide microglia. Primary human microglia are distinguished from blood-derived macrophages and other CNS cells by a homeostatic signature that includes P2RY12, GPR34, MERTK, C1QA/C1QB/C1QC, PROS1, GAS6, TMEM119, HEXB and SALL1, together with dependence on CNS-derived cues, notably TGF-β signaling, for maintenance of this program ref [1], ref [2]. Earlier work had already established that resident microglia are phenotypically separable from infiltrating myeloid cells by their characteristic low/intermediate CD45 expression and distinct antigen-presenting profile, underscoring that “microglial identity” cannot be inferred from generic myeloid markers alone ref [4].

Against this benchmark, the basal molecular profile of HMC3 appears only partially microglial. As an immortalized human microglial line, HMC3 retains expression of broadly myeloid/microglia-associated molecules reported in classical characterization studies, but immortalized microglial lines generally fail to preserve the adult homeostatic signature seen in freshly isolated microglia ref [1]. This limitation is consistent with later transcriptomic work showing that human microglial identity is strongly environment-dependent and rapidly erodes ex vivo, with marked downregulation of signature genes after transfer to standard culture conditions ref [2]. Thus, absence or weak basal expression of canonical homeostatic markers in HMC3 should not be interpreted simply as technical variability, but as a predictable consequence of long-term immortalization and non-CNS culture context ref [1], ref [2].

In practical terms, HMC3 should therefore be regarded as a human microglia-like myeloid model rather than a faithful surrogate of resting adult microglia. Basal readouts in this line are best interpreted relative to a restricted core phenotype—human origin, macrophage/microglia-related immunocompetence, and responsiveness to inflammatory cues—while claims about microglial homeostasis, disease-associated state transitions, or lineage-defining transcriptional programs require validation against primary human microglia or higher-fidelity induced models ref [2]. Careful reporting of marker panels that include both pan-myeloid and microglia-enriched genes is especially important when using HMC3 to support statements about microglial identity ref [1], ref [4].

Studies using the CHME3/C13NJ human microglial line consistently show that its morphology is highly plastic and tightly coupled to migratory signaling. In chemotaxis assays, multiple inflammatory chemokines—including MCP-1, MIP-1α/β, RANTES, IL-8, and IP-10—induce significant migration of CHME3 cells with the expected bell-shaped dose-response profile, while phalloidin staining demonstrates rapid F-actin redistribution from a predominantly perinuclear pattern toward a more polarized cytoplasmic organization associated with protrusive activity ref [31]. Complementary wound-healing and transwell studies further indicate that neurotensin is also a potent motility cue for this model, acting through neurotensin receptor-3/sortilin and requiring both PI3K/Akt and ERK signaling ref [14].

At the morphological level, stimulated cells acquire features compatible with an activated, locomotory phenotype. Chemokine exposure promotes actin polymerization and reorganization, whereas neurotensin triggers rapid formation of numerous actin-rich filopodia and increased stress fibers before measurable migration occurs ref [31], ref [14]. These observations support the view that HMC3/CHME3 can engage canonical cytoskeletal programs of surveillance-to-motile transition, even if their immortalized state and culture conditions likely constrain the full ramified repertoire seen in homeostatic primary human microglia.

HMC3/CHME3 cells also display matrix-remodeling competence that may facilitate tissue infiltration. Chemokine stimulation increases secretion of MMP-2 and, by zymography, enhances both MMP-2 and MMP-9, while also elevating TIMP-1 and TIMP-2 and reducing soluble uPA, indicating coordinated but complex control of extracellular proteolysis ref [32]. In a tuberculosis-conditioned medium model, microglia upregulate MMP-1 and MMP-3 in a dose- and time-dependent manner via p38 MAPK-dependent transcriptional programs ref [33]. Together with broader evidence that metalloproteinases are major myeloid-cell effectors in matrix turnover and barrier injury, these findings position HMC3 as a useful, if simplified, system for studying coupled motility and protease-driven remodeling phenotypes in neuroinflammatory contexts ref [5].

Phagocytosis and inflammatory polarization are among the most frequently interrogated functional outputs of HMC3/CHME3 cells. In this model, fluorescent Aβ1–42 is internalized and trafficked to lysosomal compartments, supporting its use for studying amyloid clearance mechanisms ref [34]. Importantly, Aβ uptake is not phenotypically neutral: phagocytic cells are enriched for inflammatory-associated markers such as IL-1RI and iNOS, indicating that cargo handling in HMC3 can coexist with a partially activated state rather than a purely homeostatic program ref [34].

Several studies further show that phagocytosis and inflammatory polarization can be pharmacologically dissociated. IFN-γ robustly enhances Aβ1–42 uptake in CHME3/HMC3, but simultaneously elevates IL-6 and suppresses BDNF, consistent with a trade-off between amyloid clearance and a more injurious inflammatory profile ref [34]. By contrast, omega-3 fatty acids promote a more pro-resolving configuration: DHA and EPA increase Aβ42 phagocytosis while reducing M1-associated markers (CD40, CD86), with DHA also lowering TNF-α and EPA increasing BDNF release ref [21]. In the same line, resolution-pathway profiling showed that LPS, but not Aβ42, preferentially upregulates ALX/FPR2, p-5-LOX, α7nAChR, and PPAR-δ, suggesting that amyloid exposure may drive an inflammatory state that is less competent to engage endogenous resolution programs ref [37].

Anti-inflammatory interventions in HMC3 also reveal distinct pathway dependencies. Dexmedetomidine suppresses the LPS/ATP-induced inflammasome response by reducing c-Fos-dependent NLRP3 and caspase-1 activation, with consequent decreases in IL-1β and IL-18 release ref [35]. Earlier work with statins showed more mixed effects: atorvastatin reduced basal, LPS-induced, and Aβ-induced IL-6 secretion, whereas simvastatin was less effective on cytokine suppression and both statins reduced cell viability at higher doses, emphasizing that anti-inflammatory readouts in HMC3 may be confounded by metabolic toxicity ref [6]. Overall, the literature supports HMC3 as a useful but context-sensitive model in which phagocytosis, inflammasome signaling, and M1/M2-like polarization can shift independently rather than along a single activation axis ref [34], ref [21], ref [37].

subsections.subsection_title: Innate Immune and Infection-Responsive Phenotypic States
subsections.content:
HMC3/CHME3 cells have been used extensively to model infection-responsive innate states, particularly in viral encephalitis paradigms. In hepatitis C virus antigen exposure, recombinant NS3 drives a classical pro-inflammatory response in these cells through TLR2/TLR6-MyD88-NF-κB signaling, with induction of IL-8, IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β; notably, prior conditioning with TLR ligands dampens this response and is associated with IL-10 production, highlighting a capacity for inducible innate tolerance rather than fixed activation [1].

Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) studies further show that HMC3 cells adopt highly dynamic antiviral and immunoregulatory states. Global miRNAome/transcriptome profiling revealed time-resolved rewiring of innate pathways, including Notch, cytokine, and interferon-associated programs, indicating that infection elicits coordinated rather than monotonic activation [5]. At the level of specific regulators, TRIM21 acts as a negative feedback node by restraining IRF3 phosphorylation and IFN-β production during JEV infection [6]. In parallel, miR-155 overexpression suppresses JEV replication while attenuating NF-κB-linked inflammatory outputs, IRF8 induction, and complement factor H expression, consistent with an antiviral yet immunomodulatory phenotype [4]. Conversely, miR-146a can suppress TRAF6/IRAK1/IRAK2- and STAT1-dependent signaling, reduce ISG expression, and facilitate replication in a strain-dependent manner [7], whereas JEV-driven miR-432/SOCS5 signaling further inhibits Jak-STAT responses and promotes viral persistence-related fitness [8].

Beyond JEV, HMC3 cells have also been informative for other neurotropic viruses and viral proteins. Axl, which is expressed in human microglia and astrocytes, mediates Zika virus entry and simultaneously dampens interferon-linked innate responses, underscoring how receptor usage and immune modulation are mechanistically coupled in glial infection [9]. In HIV-related models, Tat protein reshapes microglial signaling via miR-32-dependent repression of TRAF3, with downstream effects on IRF3/IRF7 signaling [10]. Collectively, these studies position HMC3 cells as a useful system for dissecting infection-triggered innate plasticity, feedback inhibition, and viral exploitation of microRNA-controlled immune checkpoints [1,4-10].

Figures in the HMC3 literature have served less to define a canonical phenotype than to visualize assay-dependent behavior. Early papers typically presented phase-contrast morphology, immunocytochemical staining for macrophage/microglial markers, and cytokine-expression readouts to support the use of immortalized human microglia-like cells in inflammatory studies ref [10], ref [11]. Subsequent figure panels frequently combined fluorescence microscopy with migration or actin-remodeling assays, illustrating that HMC3 responses are highly contingent on the stimulus and experimental endpoint rather than on a stable homeostatic microglial signature ref [31], ref [14].

A recurring pattern is the dominance of pathway-centric figures. In neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative paradigms, figures commonly depict ROS production, inflammasome activation, MMP/TIMP regulation, amyloid-β uptake, or pharmacologic modulation by statins, omega-3 fatty acids, or other anti-inflammatory compounds ref [18], ref [32], ref [34], ref [37], ref [36]. These visual datasets are useful for comparing relative responses within a study, but they often rely on a limited set of markers and 2D culture morphology, which can overstate microglial relevance if interpreted without transcriptomic or authentication context.

Accordingly, the most informative figures for future HMC3 work should go beyond representative microscopy alone. Side-by-side presentation of cell authentication, mycoplasma testing, marker panels, and benchmarking against primary or iPSC-derived human microglia would substantially improve interpretability and reproducibility ref [12], ref [2]. In a literature base marked by historical renaming and phenotype drift, figure design is therefore not merely illustrative, but central to judging the validity of HMC3-based conclusions.
